title: How Whaling Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whaling, starting with news that Japan's Antarctic whaling season ended early with 267 whales caught, attributed to Sea Shepherd's interference. They trace whaling history from Basque commercial whaling through Nantucket and New Bedford's golden age, when whale oil fueled the Industrial Revolution, to Sven Foyn's steam-powered whaling ship and explosive harpoon cannon, which devastated whale populations. They cover traditional hand-harpoon whaling, the dangers of processing whales at sea, and the 1946 ban on commercial whaling. They discuss Japan's scientific whaling loophole under Article VIII, the International Whaling Commission's lack of enforcement, and the Essex, the ship sunk by a whale that inspired Moby Dick. The episode ends with listener mail about the nonprofit Retreat America and a contest winner's visit.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor tease
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat casually about musical tastes, including classic rock, before Josh introduces the topic of whaling.

segments.title: Japan's shortened Antarctic whale hunt and Sea Shepherd
segments.summary: Japan's Antarctic whaling fleet returned early with 267 whales, short of its planned nine. Sea Shepherd's harassment is credited with ending the season early. Whaling by Alaska indigenous groups is noted, and the hosts discuss public sympathy for whales.

segments.title: Early history of commercial whaling
segments.summary: Commercial whaling is traced to the Basques in the Bay of Biscay around 1000, followed by England, North America, Japan, and the US. Nantucket becomes a whaling center, and whale oil fuels the Industrial Revolution, making New Bedford and Nantucket very wealthy from about 1750 to 1850.

segments.title: Sven Foyn and the harpoon cannon
segments.summary: Norwegian Sven Foyn launched the first steam-powered whaling ship in 1863 and invented the explosive harpoon cannon. The hosts describe hand-harpoon whaling, where whales died slowly, and how the cannon sped up killing and devastated populations. Figures from South Georgia are given.

segments.title: Whale use, dangers, and processing at sea
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how whales were used for food, fuel, and tools, and sperm whale oil and spermaceti's value. They describe the dangers of whaleboats and the diseases of whaling voyages, and the process of flensing, boiling blubber, and multi-year voyages on board.

segments.title: International regulation, the 1946 ban, and the scientific whaling loophole
segments.summary: The League of Nations and the International Agreement for the Regulation of Whaling are discussed, along with the lack of enforcement by the IWC. A commercial whaling ban followed in 1946, but Japan, Norway and Russia rejected it. The scientific whaling exemption is criticized by Greenpeace and compared with Australian research methods, and whale catch numbers have declined since then.

segments.title: Whale population recovery and the Essex
segments.summary: The hosts discuss slow whale reproduction and the race against extinction. They describe the Essex, the whaleship sunk by a whale that inspired Moby Dick, and the crew's survival and cannibalism.

segments.title: Sea Shepherd 2010 confrontation
segments.summary: The hosts recount a 2010 incident in which a Japanese ship allegedly rammed a Sea Shepherd vessel, and Sea Shepherd crew boarded the whaling ship, with no meaningful outcome.

segments.title: Listener mail: Retreat America and a contest winner
segments.summary: Listener Patrick writes about Retreat America, a tree-planting and bicycle nonprofit formed after the 2011 Bastrop wildfires. The hosts also recall taking Facebook contest winner Caleb to lunch and to the office.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The hosts ask for listener whaling stories and give contact details and a video podcast plug.
